idea.why: Genuine decomposition: a triage specialist, a scheduling specialist, and an editor that consumes both structured outputs and writes only the body. Each domain follows the same sensible three-beat shape so the model is called once per domain rather than per message.

structure.why: Well chosen types and a proportionate count, with one shared model serving all three agents. The gap: three agents are told to emit strict JSON by prompt alone, with no structured parser attached, which is precisely the purpose-built component for that job.

connections.why: The wiring does not express the real dependencies. Two wholly independent sources, yet the calendar fetch waits on the email fetch, the aggregate and the triage agent, producing a flat nine-deep chain where a fan-out plus a Merge is the honest graph. Credit where due: the model port is correctly fanned out to all three agents, so the author knew how to express one-to-many and simply did not apply it on the main path.

answer.why: End to end this is what was asked, with empty cases specified in both prompts and subjects told to be escaped. Small shortfalls: presents resolves to a draft the user must go open, and one stray fence from the editor would land verbatim inside the template with nothing to catch it.

appraisal: The decomposition is the strong part: three genuinely specialised agents over one shared model, each domain aggregated to a single item so the model runs once, and a template node holding the chrome so the editor only writes body fragments. The output is a dashboard a person would actually read, safely parked as a draft. The weak dimension is the wiring: two unrelated fetches strung into one nine-deep chain, and the point where mail and calendar genuinely rejoin is papered over with a reach-back instead of a Merge. The first change is to fan out and merge; the second is to hang a structured parser off the two JSON-emitting agents.
